title: The number row
summary: Ten keys in one lesson, from the middle of the row outward, anchored to the home key below each one.
intro: The number row is the furthest your fingers ever reach, and the only row you will type without any hope of feeling your way back — there are no bumps up there. What makes it work is the anchor: every digit belongs to the finger directly below it, so 4 is the F finger, 7 is the J finger, 1 is the A finger. Learn each digit against its home key and the row stops being a guess.
congrats: Ten keys in one lesson, and you kept your hands on the home row through all of them. Dates, prices, phone numbers and house numbers are now things you can type without looking down — which is most of what anybody actually uses the number row for.

screens.text: Left index finger, up two rows from F. Start in the middle of the row where the reach is shortest, and keep the other three fingers touching their home keys as it goes.
Both of these belong to the left index finger: 4 straight up, 5 up and inward. Press the digit, then its home key, so the finger learns the way back.
The mirror on the right hand. 6 is a long inward reach and the one people most often give to the wrong hand — it belongs to the right index finger.
The four middle digits, alternating. Say each one to yourself as you type it; naming the key is what stops the finger guessing.
Middle fingers now. Straight up from D and K, and straight back down — the same movement they make for E and I, just one row further.
Ring fingers, which are the least independent you have. Watch the little finger beside each one: if it lifts off its home key, the reach is coming from the hand, not the finger.
The little fingers and the longest reach on the keyboard. These two are worth going slowly for — they are also the two you will use most, because every year and every price has a 1 or a 0 in it.
The outer digits mixed with the ones you learned first. Accuracy matters more here than anywhere else in the course: a wrong letter is a typo, a wrong digit is a wrong number.
The whole row in order, then in pairs from the outside in. Keep your eyes on the screen rather than hunting along the row.

screens.text: Digits inside ordinary phrases, which is where you will actually meet them. Notice how your hand has to come back to the home row between the numbers and the words.
Whole numbers rather than single digits. Type each one as a shape rather than as four separate keys — that is how you will read them back.
